text: One in 500 people has this disease. A test catches 99% of cases and wrongly flags 1% of the healthy. If yours says positive, what's the chance you're sick? Pick a number. Most doctors given a problem like this got it wrong. The tempting answer is the test's own hit rate, 99%. You'd start treatment today. Check that rule by counting. Here are 10,000 people and suppose half of them are sick. Test everyone. 99% of the sick light up, and 1% of the healthy. Of the 5,000 who lit up, 99% are sick. Here, the rule holds. Now make the disease rare, like yours, one in 500. That leaves 20 sick people. Run the same test. About 20 sick people light up, plus 1% of the 9,980 healthy ones. That's about 100. So of 120 positives, only 20 are sick. That's 17%. The rule said 99, six times too high. 1% sounds small, but here it's 1% of nearly everyone. Your positive result ruled out everyone who tested negative. What's left is a smaller sample space, these 120 people. Your chance of being sick is the red share of this crowd. 20 out of 20 plus 100. Before rounding, these are 19.8 and 99.8. That's 20 sick people times 99% and 9980 healthy times 1%. Divide top and bottom by 10,000. The share stays the same but each headcount becomes a fraction of everyone two in a thousand and nine hundred ninety eight in a thousand these two say how common each group is these two how often each group tests positive that's Bayes theorem all it does is shrink the sample space to what the evidence allows then take the share as for those gynecologists after one session turning percentages into counts of women, the way we just counted people, 87% got it right. Swap the disease for a police watch list. At the 2017 Champions League final, about 170,000 people were in Cardiff. The watch lists held about 1,200 faces, so even a small error rate per face would swamp the real matches. Face recognition cameras scanned the crowd and raised 2,470 alerts. Police counted 173 as right, 7%. In machine learning, the share of alerts that are right is called precision. Later, a new algorithm and better photos cut the false alarms, and 46% of alerts were judged right. Back to your test. The title's 99% accuracy is real, but a test that calls Everyone Healthy scores 99.8, more accurate and useless. Your 17% assumes a random screen. Symptoms raise the 1 in 500, and the answer climbs. 50% at 1 in 100, 99 at 1 in 2 were the rule held. On a random screen, 20 reach this plus along the red, 100 along the blue. 99% is the test's recall, how often the sick test positive. 17% is its precision, how often the positive are sick.
